proposal.description_long: Ontario’s provincial government sponsored an advertisement using excerpts from former President Ronald Reagan’s 1987 radio address about tariffs. On Oct. 23, 2025, President Donald Trump called the ad “FAKE” on Truth Social, said it was intended to interfere with pending tariff litigation, and announced that he was terminating all trade negotiations with Canada. The Associated Press reported that the ad was sponsored by Ontario, a Canadian province, rather than Canada’s federal government. On Oct. 24, Trump told reporters, “I guess it was AI or something,” framing AI as a suggestion rather than presenting production evidence. FactCheck.org compared the ad with Reagan’s address and found that the ad rearranged portions and omitted context but did not change Reagan’s broader criticism of tariffs. The reviewed sources document Trump’s accusation and the trade-talk announcement; they do not establish that artificial intelligence generated the ad or what happened to later negotiations. This proposed event is limited to Trump’s public response and decision over the Ontario advertisement.

staged_record.description_long: The dispute began with an Ontario government advertisement that used excerpts from Ronald Reagan’s 1987 radio address criticizing tariffs. The speech was real, though the ad edited and rearranged portions of it and did not include the full context of Reagan’s comments about tariffs on Japan. On October 23, 2025, President Donald Trump called the ad fake, said it interfered with Supreme Court cases over his tariffs, and announced that he was ending trade negotiations with Canada. A day later, he said he guessed it was made using AI, an allegation for which the contemporaneous reporting cited here offered no supporting production evidence. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the province would pause the ad after its initial World Series broadcasts. On October 25, Trump announced an additional 10% tariff on Canadian goods. Reporting did not make clear which products would be covered or how the increase would interact with existing exemptions for qualifying goods under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement. The episode tied a political advertisement to a breakdown in trade talks and a new tariff threat, but it does not establish whether negotiations later resumed or what the tariff’s eventual economic effect was.
